Mike Strange recorded and mixed Eminem's vocals at Effigy Studios in Ferndale, Michigan.[19] The sessions took two days.[20] Strange edited the vocals with D-Verb—a reverberation software—and an Extra Long Delay plug-in. He preferred to make few changes; for "Love the Way You Lie" he almost exclusively used board compression and console equalization. Strange used the Bricasti and Eventide Reverb 2016 mixing tools for "brighter" reverberation. Detroit musician Luis Resto has contributed to the arrangement on many of Eminem's songs, but did not do so for "Love the Way You Lie". According to Strange, "Everything we needed was already in the track, apart from the vocals."[2] Two to three weeks after the sessions, Alex da Kid arrived to help mix and master the track.[11] He wanted to replace the acoustic guitar on the demo, but Eminem chose to keep it.[3] Strange said, "It was simply a matter of trying to match and then to improve on the demo [Alex da Kid]'d sent us."[2] Strange's brother Joe engineered the track.[19]

Rihanna's recording sessions took place at Sun Studios in Dublin, Ireland, and were engineered by Marcos Tovar. The R&B songwriter Makeba Riddick provided additional vocal production.[19] Strange used equalization, compression and reverberation but left the vocal balance. He assumed that Rihanna was satisfied with her recorded vocals and did not make major changes on her seven stereo vocal tracks.[2]

Release and response
On May 27, 2010, Eminem revealed the title of "Love the Way You Lie" as part of the track list of his seventh studio album Recovery,[35] which came out on June 21.[36] Initially a radio single,[37] the song was released later by Polydor Records as a CD in the United Kingdom on August 9, 2010.[1] Interscope Records distributed it in Germany on August 20.[38]

"Love the Way You Lie" received generally favorable reviews. An editor for Rap-Up listed it among the four best tracks from the album.[39] New York Times writer Jon Caramanica considered it "one of the album's most engaging songs" and praised Eminem's ability to assess issues from the perspectives of both sexes.[40] MTV's Rodriguez wrote that the song echoes content from Eminem's earlier albums, but finds him "sober" and "more mature".[41] He added that the lyrics allude to Eminem's relationship with Scott and that "Love the Way You Lie" is his closest approach to a love song.[30] Editors of The A.V. Club compared the single with "Kim" and "'97 Bonnie & Clyde"; they found he is more tempered in "Love the Way You Lie" when discussing a "mutually destructive relationship" and that Rihanna's involvement creates an eerie mood.[42]

Critics especially praised Rihanna's contribution. Michael Menachem of Billboard complimented her "exquisitely melodic and surprisingly hopeful" vocal performance and "Eminem's dark, introspective" rapping.[25] He noted that the percussion complements both artists and that Alex da Kid gave the classical arrangement a mainstream touch.[25] Kyle Anderson, writing for MTV, remarked that the song showcases Rihanna's emotional vocals and Eminem's "most intense rhymes about his tumultuous relationships".[43] He regarded "Love the Way You Lie" as an honest, "well-constructed pop song with a killer hook" and likened the "slow-burning" music to that of "Someone like You", a 2011 single by the British singer Adele.[43][44] The Houston Chronicle pop critic Joey Guerra commented that Rihanna brought a "sandpaper and silk sheen" to the track.[45]"

The single sold over 12 million copies in the US and 1.5 million in the UK. Musical acts such as Cher Lloyd and the Band Perry have performed cover versions. Trần Thủ Độ's controversial reputation in Vietnamese history stems from two pivotal actions that combined political ruthlessness with moral ambiguity. First, he orchestrated the **forced marriage between Trần Thái Tông and Princess Thuận Thiên**, the wife of his brother Trần Liễu. This marriage was arranged to secure power for Trần Thái Tông, who was a minor at the time, and it resulted in the forced abdication of Lý Chiêu Hoàng, the Empress Regnant. The union was deeply resented by Trần Liễu, who viewed it as a betrayal, leading to a revolt that Trần Thủ Độ quelled with extreme measures, including the execution of rebels and the suppression of dissent. This act, while critical to establishing the Trần dynasty, was widely criticized by historians like Ngô Sĩ Liên and Phan Phu Tiên, who saw it as a catalyst for later dynastic instability.

Nguyễn Trãi's choice to name his work *Bình Ngô Đại Cáo* ("Pacification of the Wu") rather than directly referencing the Ming Dynasty reflects a deliberate rhetorical and historical strategy. This decision is rooted in both the political context of the time and the symbolic significance of the term "Wu" (吳). Here’s a breakdown of the reasoning:

### 1. **Historical and Cultural Context of "Wu"**  
The term "Wu" (吳) refers to the ancient state of Wu, a historical kingdom in southern China that existed during the Three Kingdoms period (220–280 CE). Zhu Yuanzhang, the founder of the Ming Dynasty, was born in Hao Prefecture (modern-day Fengyang, Anhui), which was part of the former state of Wu. By invoking "Wu," Nguyễn Trãi subtly linked the Ming Dynasty to its historical origins, avoiding direct confrontation with the Ming while still acknowledging their rule over Đại Việt. This allowed him to frame the Ming as a continuation of a historical entity rather than an external foreign power, which may have softened the document’s tone of resistance.

### 2. **Avoiding Direct Naming of the Ming Dynasty**  
Naming the work *Pacification of the Ming* would have been overtly confrontational, potentially alienating readers or inviting censorship. By using "Wu," Nguyễn Trãi could bypass the need to explicitly name the Ming, which was politically sensitive during the early 15th century. This choice also aligned with the tradition of using historical references to critique contemporary rulers without direct accusation, a common practice in Confucian scholarship.

### 3. **Symbolic Framing of Victory**  
The term "Wu" carried connotations of a regional power that had once been a rival to the northern dynasties of China. By associating the Ming with "Wu," Nguyễn Trãi implicitly positioned Đại Việt as reclaiming its sovereignty from a historically peripheral entity. This framing emphasized the legitimacy of the Lam Sơn uprising as a restoration of national independence rather than a mere rebellion against a foreign occupier. It also reinforced the idea that Đại Việt’s independence was a continuation of its ancient traditions, not a new creation.

### 4. **Literary and Political Significance of "Đại Cáo"**  
The term "đại cáo" (大誥) in the title refers to a type of imperial edict used by the Ming Dynasty to legitimize its rule. By adopting this term, Nguyễn Trãi subverted its original meaning. Instead of using it to assert the authority of the Ming, he repurposed it to declare the victory of Đại Việt and the failure of the Ming’s rule. This inversion of meaning transformed the document into a declaration of independence, symbolizing the triumph of Đại Việt’s sovereignty over the Ming’s imperial ambitions.

### 5. **Cultural and Nationalist Resonance**  
The use of "Wu" also resonated with Vietnamese historical narratives that emphasized the distinction between the northern Chinese dynasties and the southern Vietnamese polity. By referencing "Wu," Nguyễn Trãi tapped into a shared cultural memory of resistance against northern domination, aligning the Lam Sơn uprising with the broader tradition of Vietnamese patriotism. This choice helped solidify the document’s role as a cornerstone of Vietnamese national identity, linking it to the legacy of figures like Lý Thường Kiệt and the poem *Nam Quốc Sơn Hà*.

In summary, Nguyễn Trãi’s choice of "Pacification of the Wu" was a calculated blend of historical reference, political prudence, and symbolic rhetoric. It allowed him to critique the Ming Dynasty while avoiding direct confrontation, frame the victory as a restoration of sovereignty, and reinforce the legitimacy of Đại Việt’s independence through cultural and literary means. This decision underscores the strategic depth of his work, which remains a defining text of Vietnamese resistance literature.

The **Hồ Dynasty** was ruled by two monarchs: **Hồ Quý Ly** (also known as Lê Quý Ly during his early life) and his son **Hồ Hán Thương**. Hồ Quý Ly founded the dynasty in the early 15th century, establishing it as a short-lived but influential regime in Vietnamese history. His son, Hồ Hán Thương, succeeded him as the second emperor, though his reign was brief and marked by the dynasty's eventual downfall.  

The official title of the Hồ Dynasty was **Đại Ngu** (Vietnamese: *Đại Ngu*; Chinese: *大虞*), which translates to "Great Peace." This name was adopted by Hồ Quý Ly after he seized power, likely inspired by his claimed descent from the ancient Chinese Emperor Shun (虞舜), whom he associated with the concept of "Great Peace." The title reflected his ambition to restructure governance and assert cultural and political independence from Chinese influence.  

The dynasty's brief existence (c. 1399–1407) was characterized by efforts to centralize power, promote the use of **Chữ Nôm** (the Vietnamese script), and assert control over territories previously held by the Trần Dynasty and Champa. However, internal instability and external pressures, particularly the Ming Dynasty's invasion in 1407, led to its collapse. The official title **Đại Ngu** remains a key identifier of this period in Vietnamese history.

The Trần dynasty's authority and power in the 1370s and 1380s declined steadily after Trần Nghệ Tông's reign (1370–1372). He had ceded the throne in favor of his son Trần Duệ Tông (r. 1372–77), his grandson Trần Phế Đế (r. 1377–88), and Trần Thuận Tông (r. 1388–98), one of his younger sons.

The practice of bequeathing the throne to a designated son (not simply passing it on to the eldest) was similar to what had happened in the previous Trần dynasty and was meant to avoid sibling rivalry. Origin and background
The Hồ/Hú family originated around modern-day Zhejiang province in the Southern Tang dynasty, which controlled much of southeast China, around the 940s. China was then in the midst of the chaotic Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period. The Hồ claimed descent from Duke Hu of Chen (Trần Hồ công, 陳胡公), who in turn was descended from the ancient Chinese Emperor Shun (Thuấn, 舜).  Under Hồ Liêm (胡廉), Hồ Quý Ly's great-great-grandfather, the family migrated south from the Southern Tang until they established themselves in northern Vietnam. Hồ Liêm moved further south and settled in Thanh Hóa Province (about 100 km south of the modern city of Hanoi). Some historians bring attention to the fact that Hồ Quý Ly is also known as Lê Quý Ly. In his childhood, Hồ Quý Ly was adopted by Lê Huan, and took his family name. He did not change his family name from Lê back to Hồ until after he had deposed the last king of the Trần dynasty. Because of the short span of the Hồ dynasty and the tragic circumstances they brought upon the country, the family name "Hồ" was disgraced thereafter. However, historians have attributed to the Hồ family quite a few notable scholars, dignitaries, and government officials under both the Lý dynasty and the Trần dynasty.

Hồ Quý Ly's ascent to power
The Trần dynasty's authority and power in the 1370s and 1380s declined steadily after Trần Nghệ Tông's reign (1370–1372). He had ceded the throne in favor of his son Trần Duệ Tông (r. 1372–77), his grandson Trần Phế Đế (r. 1377–88), and Trần Thuận Tông (r. 1388–98), one of his younger sons.
The Trần dynasty became known for emperors who reigned for only a few years before relinquishing the throne to a favorite son and becoming Thái Thượng Hoàng Đế, the first dynasty to take the name of Father of "Hoàng Đế" emperor title. Coup d'état of Hồ Quý Ly (1399)

To facilitate his takeover, Hồ Quý Ly first had a new capital built, called Tây Đô (literally "Western Capital"). In 1399, he invited the current emperor, Trần Thuận Tông, to visit this new capital. After coaxing the emperor into relinquishing the throne to Prince An (a three-year-old child) he had Trần Thuận Tông imprisoned in a pagoda and later executed. Prince An "reigned" for one year until Hồ Quý Ly deposed him in 1400 and declared himself to be the new emperor.

Under the Hồ dynasty, the Chữ nôm script was promoted by the Hồ over Classical Chinese to write the vernacular Vietnamese language.

Final years
In 1402 the army of the Hồ dynasty under general Đỗ Mãn made significant inroads against Champa, prompting the Champa king to cede large territory to Vietnam.

The song follows a chord progression of E♭m7–C♭maj9–G♭–B♭m with a tempo of 125 beats per minute, and the vocals span from A♭3 to G♭5. According to Warren, she was told in the early years of her career to never write a song where the male partner will not "get it", but later stopped following that because she thinks the "best writing" happens when she stops worrying about what to do and just expresses herself. She added that she applied this approach with "New Rules", whose lyrics were inspired by Ailin's struggles with the temptation of getting back together with a former boyfriend. The song was passed down by a few artists, including one who thought it did not have a notable hook.
